title: Case study: unique ID generator
summary: 64-bit time-ordered ids with no coordinator on the hot path: the bit budget, a sequence that never wraps, clocks that step backwards, and node ids as leases with tokens, deadlines and floors.

units.title: Guided design: requirements, bit budget, API and model, candidates and HLD, three deep dives (sequence, clock, node ids)

labs.title: Time + node + sequence ids: bit layout, a concurrent generator with overflow and clock-regression handling, node-id leases with tokens, deadlines and floors

outcomes.text: Scope an id-generator prompt in ≤ 6 minutes: uniqueness scope, size (64 bits, and 2^53 for JavaScript), the strength of ordering (none, k-sorted, per-producer, total), rates and bursts, processes and regions, behaviour during coordination outages, information leakage and gaps, and say which box each answer moves.

Estimate the bit budget: time bits from the tick and lifetime (and the end date for a given epoch), node bits from processes plus churn, sequence bits from the hottest producer, and key bytes saved against 128-bit ids, and tie each number to a decision.

Design the API and data model: an in-process library that returns errors instead of guesses, a batch service for clients that can't embed it, ids as strings in JSON, and the node-lease record (token, expiry, high-water).

Compare UUIDv4, UUIDv7/ULID, database sequences with interleaved offsets, ticket servers, leased ranges and time + node + sequence on size, ordering, coordination per id, dependency failure and index locality, and defend a choice with a flip condition.
Explain sequence overflow policies (wait, borrow within a bound, error; never wrap), why k-sorted is not linearizable, and why id % N sharding concentrates load on one shard.
Choose a clock-regression policy (wait out small steps, refuse large ones, bounded run-ahead, a floor at startup) for slews, steps, leap seconds, resumed VMs and restarts, and say what each costs.
Assign node ids safely with leases: a fencing token per grant, a holder-side deadline measured from the send time, a floor for the next holder, and a TTL sized against registry outages and churn.

Implement the layout, a concurrent generator with overflow and regression handling, a lease registry and a leased worker, and show with break-its what a naive generator, a shared node id and a paused holder do (labs/c3/snowflake).
Explain index locality of random vs time-ordered keys, why time-ordered ids must not lead a range-partition key, and what ordering ids from several regions really have.
